title: Momentum, impulse, and collisions: vector conservation in action
summary: Signs matter: momentum is a vector. See why stretching impact time saves lives with airbags, how momentum stays conserved in every isolated collision, and what separates elastic from inelastic hits.

m1.label: $m_1$
m1.meaning: mass of cart A, in kilograms (kg)
m1.body: Multiplies cart A's velocity to give its momentum, and joins $m_2$ after the two carts lock together.
m1.analogy: The heavier cart entering from the left.

u1.label: $u_1$
u1.meaning: initial velocity of cart A (to the right, positive), in m/s
u1.body: Positive because we choose right as the $+$ direction. Always set a {sign_convention|sign convention} first.
u1.analogy: Cart A's arrow pointing right before the hit.

m2.label: $m_2$
m2.meaning: mass of cart B, in kilograms (kg)
m2.body: Smaller than $m_1$, yet moving head-on so its negative momentum cancels part of cart A's momentum.
m2.analogy: The lighter oncoming cart from the right.

u2.label: $u_2$
u2.meaning: initial velocity of cart B (to the left, negative), in m/s
u2.body: Carries a **minus sign** because it moves opposite to the chosen positive direction. Dropping this sign ruins the answer.
u2.analogy: Cart B's arrow pointing left, opposing cart A.

dt.label: $\Delta t$
dt.meaning: contact duration of the collision, in seconds (s)
dt.body: Links {impulse|impulse} to average impact force via $F_{\text{avg}} = I / \Delta t$. Longer contact means smaller peak force.
dt.example: A padded bumper stretches the collision to $\Delta t = 0.2\text{ s}$.
dt.analogy: How long the bumpers stay pressed together during the crunch.

p_tot.label: $\Sigma p$
p_tot.meaning: total vector momentum of the two-cart system, in kg·m/s
p_tot.body: By {conservation_momentum|conservation of momentum}, $\Sigma p$ before the hit equals $\Sigma p$ after whenever external net force is zero.
p_tot.analogy: The combined directional push carried by the pair as a whole.

v_after.label: $v$
v_after.meaning: common velocity of the coupled carts after impact, in m/s
v_after.body: Both carts share this single velocity because they lock together. Its sign tells you which way the pair moves.
v_after.analogy: The speed and direction of the stuck-together wreck right after impact.

imp.label: $I$
imp.meaning: impulse delivered to cart A during the hit, in N·s
imp.body: Equals cart A's change in momentum: {impulse|$I = m_1 v - m_1 u_1$}. Cart B receives the exact opposite impulse $-I$.
imp.analogy: The total jolt cart B delivers to cart A.

f_avg.label: $F_{\text{avg}}$
f_avg.meaning: average impact force on cart A during contact, in newtons (N)
f_avg.body: Found from {newton_second|Newton's second law} in impulse form: $F_{\text{avg}} = I / \Delta t$. By {newton_third|Newton's third law}, cart B feels $-F_{\text{avg}}$.
f_avg.analogy: How hard the bumper actually shoves cart A during the crunch.

dk.label: $\Delta E_k$
dk.meaning: change in total kinetic energy of the two-cart system, in joules (J)
dk.body: Zero only in an elastic collision. In a {collision_types|completely inelastic collision}, $\Delta E_k < 0$ because mechanical energy becomes sound, heat, and deformation.
dk.analogy: The kinetic energy spent crumpling the bumpers and making a loud bang.

collision_types.title: Elastic vs inelastic collisions
collision_types.body: In an isolated collision ($\Sigma F_{\text{ext}} = 0$), total {momentum|momentum} is **always** conserved. Only an **elastic** collision also conserves total {kinetic_energy|kinetic energy}.
collision_types.says: Elastic: $\Delta E_k = 0$. Inelastic: $\Delta E_k < 0$. Completely inelastic: bodies stick together ($v_1 = v_2 = v$) and lose the maximum kinetic energy allowed by momentum conservation.
collision_types.useWhen: deciding whether you may write $E_{k,\text{before}} = E_{k,\text{after}}$ — never assume it unless the problem states the collision is elastic.

sign_convention.title: Fix the positive direction first
sign_convention.body: Both {momentum|momentum} and {impulse|impulse} are vectors. Pick one direction as $+$ before substituting numbers, and give every opposite velocity a minus sign.
sign_convention.says: Rebounding flips $+u$ to $-v$, so $\Delta p = m(-v - u)$ has a **larger** magnitude than stopping dead ($0 - mu$).
sign_convention.useWhen: objects meet head-on, recoil, or bounce off a wall.

sections.title: Force over time changes momentum
sections.body:
Work asked how far a force pushes; {impulse|impulse} asks **how long** it pushes. Multiply average force by contact time [dt:$\Delta t$] and you get the change in {momentum|momentum}: $\vec{F}_{\text{avg}}\Delta t = \Delta\vec{p}$.

When two objects collide with no outside horizontal force, {newton_third|Newton's third law} guarantees they push each other with equal and opposite forces for the exact same [dt:$\Delta t$]. Their impulses cancel in pairs, giving {conservation_momentum|conservation of momentum} — even when bumpers crumple and {kinetic_energy|kinetic energy} is lost.

sections.title: Types of isolated collisions
sections.note: momentum is conserved in all three; kinetic energy is conserved only in the first

head: Collision type
Total momentum

After impact
rows: Bounce apart with no permanent deformation
Separate, but some energy turns into heat and sound
Stick together and move at one [v_after:common velocity]

sections.title: The problem
sections.body:
On a frictionless horizontal track, cart A ([m1:$m_1 = 3\text{ kg}$]) moves right at [u1:$u_1 = +8\text{ m/s}$] and collides head-on with cart B ([m2:$m_2 = 2\text{ kg}$]) moving left at [u2:$u_2 = -7\text{ m/s}$]. The two carts lock together during an impact lasting [dt:$\Delta t = 0.2\text{ s}$].

Find (a) their [v_after:common velocity $v$] after impact, (b) the [imp:impulse $I$] and [f_avg:average impact force $F_{\text{avg}}$] on cart A, and (c) the [dk:kinetic energy change $\Delta E_k$] of the system.

sections.title: Break the problem down
sections.note: assign signs before writing a single equation

rows.note: Choose right as $+$ using the {sign_convention|sign convention}.
Moving left gives a **negative** velocity and negative initial momentum.

rows.text: Frictionless track, carts lock together in [dt:$\Delta t = 0.2\text{ s}$]
rows.note: $\Sigma F_{\text{ext}} = 0$ means {conservation_momentum|momentum is conserved}; locking together marks a {collision_types|completely inelastic collision}.
Solve for [v_after:$v$] first, then compute impulse, force, and energy loss.

sections.title: Plan
sections.note: three routes; watch out for missing minus signs and wrong energy assumptions

routes.title: Route A
routes.path: [p_tot:$\Sigma p$] with signs → [v_after:$v$] → [imp:$I$] and [f_avg:$F_{\text{avg}}$] → check [dk:$\Delta E_k$]
routes.why: {conservation_momentum|Conservation of momentum} holds for every isolated collision, including ones where carts stick together.
routes.whyNot: Nothing. This is the exact method.

routes.title: Route B
routes.why: Adds both speeds as positive numbers.
routes.whyNot: Violates the {sign_convention|sign convention}: cart B moves left, so its momentum is $-14$, not $+14$.

routes.title: Route C
routes.why: Uses conservation of energy from the previous topic.
routes.whyNot: Locking together is a {collision_types|completely inelastic collision}: most of the kinetic energy turns into heat and deformation, so $E_k$ is NOT conserved.

sections.notUsed: Vertical forces: weight and the track's normal force cancel on each cart, leaving zero net external horizontal force.

sections.title: Work it through
sections.note: keep every plus and minus sign intact

steps.move: Find the [p_tot:total momentum] before collision, taking right as $+$.
steps.why: {momentum|Momentum} is a vector; opposing directions partially cancel each other.
steps.whyNot: Do not add $24 + 14 = 38$: cart B's velocity is $-7\text{ m/s}$, not $+7\text{ m/s}$.

steps.move: Apply {conservation_momentum|conservation of momentum} to find the [v_after:common velocity] after locking together.
steps.why: Both carts share one velocity [v_after:$v$], so they act as one combined mass of $5\text{ kg}$. The $+$ sign means the pair moves right.
steps.whyNot: Do not divide by $m_1$ alone; both carts move together after the hit.

steps.move: Compute the [imp:impulse] on cart A alone.
steps.why: By {impulse|$I = \Delta p = mv - mu$}, cart A slows from $+8$ to $+2\text{ m/s}$, so the impulse pushes it to the left ($-$).
steps.whyNot: Do not swap initial and final ($u - v$): impulse is always **final minus initial**.

steps.move: Divide impulse by [dt:contact time] to find the [f_avg:average impact force] on cart A.
steps.why: From {newton_second|Newton's second law} ($F_{\text{avg}} = \Delta p / \Delta t$), cart B pushes cart A left with an average force of $90\text{ N}$.
steps.whyNot: Do not multiply by $0.2$: shorter contact time makes the force **larger**, so $\Delta t$ belongs in the denominator.

steps.move: Compare total {kinetic_energy|kinetic energy} before and after to find [dk:$\Delta E_k$].
steps.why: Kinetic energy uses speed squared, so both carts start with positive $E_k$ ($96 + 49 = 145\text{ J}$). Only $10\text{ J}$ remains; $135\text{ J}$ became heat, sound, and deformation.
steps.whyNot: Do not make cart B's initial kinetic energy negative: $(-7)^2 = +49$, so $E_k$ is never negative.

sections.title: Why airbags and crumple zones reduce impact force
sections.note: for the same impulse m|Δv|, stretching collision time Δt sharply drops average force

sections.title: Check yourself
items: **Newton's third law check**: impulse on cart B is $2(2) - 2(-7) = 4 + 14 = +18\text{ N}\cdot\text{s} = -$[imp:$I$], and average force on cart B is $+18 / 0.2 = +90\text{ N} = -$[f_avg:$F_{\text{avg}}$].

**Direction check**: cart A brought $+24\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ right while cart B brought $-14\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$ left, so the net $+10$ means the locked carts must move right ([v_after:$+2\text{ m/s}$]).
**Energy check**: [dk:$\Delta E_k = -135\text{ J} < 0$] confirms mechanical energy dropped — never positive in a passive collision.

**Airbag rule**: doubling [dt:$\Delta t$] for the same [imp:impulse] cuts [f_avg:$|F_{\text{avg}}|$] in **half** (drag $\Delta t$ from $0.2\text{ s}$ to $0.4\text{ s}$ and watch $90\text{ N}$ fall to $45\text{ N}$).

questions.q: A $0.5\text{ kg}$ rubber ball hits a wall at $+10\text{ m/s}$ and rebounds straight back at $-8\text{ m/s}$. What is the {impulse|impulse} on the ball?
questions.why: Keep the minus sign on the rebound velocity: $I = m(v - u) = 0.5(-8 - 10) = 0.5(-18) = -9\text{ N}\cdot\text{s}$.

questions.q: How does a car airbag protect a driver during a crash?
options: It reduces the driver's total momentum change $\Delta p$ to nearly zero
It increases the stopping time $\Delta t$, reducing average impact force $F_{\text{avg}} = \Delta p / \Delta t$ for the same $\Delta p$
It bounces the driver backward so the impulse cancels out
questions.why: The driver still goes from driving speed to $0$, so $\Delta p$ is the same. Stretching $\Delta t$ lowers the average force on the body.

questions.q: A $4000\text{ kg}$ truck and a $1000\text{ kg}$ car collide head-on. How does the magnitude of the impact force on the car compare with the force on the truck?
options: The force on the car is $4$ times larger because the truck is $4$ times heavier
The force on the truck is larger because the truck has more momentum
questions.why: By {newton_third|Newton's third law}, the forces are equal and opposite. The lighter car suffers $4$ times larger acceleration ($a = F/m$), not a larger force.

questions.q: Two carts on a frictionless track collide and stick together. Which quantity is conserved during this {collision_types|completely inelastic collision}?
options: Both total momentum and total kinetic energy
Total momentum only; total kinetic energy decreases
Total kinetic energy only; total momentum decreases because they slow down
questions.why: With zero external net force, total momentum is conserved, while sticking together converts part of the kinetic energy into heat, sound, and deformation.
